---
title: "The Fixed Income Sleeve"
metadata:
  pagetitle: "The Fixed Income Sleeve"
  description-meta: "Bonds as exposures to the level, slope and curvature of the yield curve and to credit spreads: measuring the exposures, targeting duration with a factor exposure constraint in PortfolioAnalytics, and a term-spread duration overlay as a parametric policy, in R."
---



What changes in portfolio construction when the asset has a duration?
@litterman1991 answered that three common factors, the level, the slope and
the curvature of the yield curve, explain nearly all of the variation in
government bond returns, so that a bond portfolio is described better by its
exposures to those factors than by the list of bonds it holds. The curve itself
has the three-parameter form of @nelson1987, which @diebold2006 turned into a
dynamic model whose factors carry the same three names. This chapter is about
the fixed income sleeve, the bond part of the allocation one level below the
class series on which @sec-15-hierarchical-allocation-theory allocates, and
its claim is that duration targeting and portfolio optimization are the same
problem in different clothes.

We first derive why a bond is a set of exposures rather than a return series,
and what credit and currency add; then measure the exposures of the government
and credit instruments of the modeled market on the curve factors that ship
with it, build a sleeve whose duration is a constraint, and fit a duration
overlay as a parametric policy; then run the sleeves out of sample against the
class series the allocation sees. On the horizon axis of
@sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory the duration decision is
**strategic**, a level of exposure held for the long run, and the positioning
along the curve that the overlay varies with the term spread is **tactical**.

The data are the weekly curve factors of `sim_curve_weekly` and the bond
instruments of `sim_asset_returns_weekly`, both described in
@sec-02-notation-and-data-simulated-market and @sec-90-data-description;
monthly instrument and class series enter in the application. Everything is in
dollars, unhedged, and the hedged return of a foreign bond is its unhedged
return less the matching `fx_return`, @eq-02-hedge.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
bonds <- dplyr::filter(sim_assets, asset_class %in% c("government", "credit"))
A  <- as_xts_pm(dplyr::filter(sim_asset_returns_weekly, asset %in% bonds$asset_id),
                date, asset, return)                               # 45 bond instruments, weekly
cv <- sim_curve_weekly |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = series, values_from = value) |>
  dplyr::arrange(date)                                             # 25 curve series, weekly
fx <- sim_fx_weekly |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(id_cols = date, names_from = region, values_from = fx_return) |>
  dplyr::arrange(date)
Am <- as_xts_pm(dplyr::filter(sim_asset_returns_monthly, asset %in% bonds$asset_id),
                date, asset, return)                               # the same instruments, monthly
R  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)    # sixteen risky classes
rf <- sim_riskfree_monthly$return                                  # the bill
wk <- as.Date(zoo::index(A)); dates <- zoo::index(R); Tn <- length(dates)
stopifnot(ncol(A) == 45L, nrow(cv) == nrow(A) + 1L, all(cv$date[-1] == wk),
          all(fx$date == wk), identical(zoo::index(Am), dates), !anyNA(A))
```
:::


The curve table has one week more than the return table: it starts a week
earlier, so that a change in the curve exists for the first return.

## Bonds as Exposures to the Curve {#sec-22-fixed-income-sleeve-theory}

### Price, duration and the return decomposition

A zero-coupon bond paying one unit at maturity $\tau$ has, at a continuously
compounded yield $y_t(\tau)$, the price

$$
P_t(\tau) = e^{-\tau\, y_t(\tau)} .
$$ {#eq-22-price}

Hold it for a period $\Delta$. It ages to maturity $\tau-\Delta$ and is priced
at the new yield for that maturity, so the log return is exactly

$$
\log\frac{P_{t+\Delta}(\tau-\Delta)}{P_t(\tau)}
= \underbrace{\Delta\, y_t(\tau)}_{\text{carry}}
+ \underbrace{(\tau-\Delta)\big[y_t(\tau) - y_t(\tau-\Delta)\big]}_{\text{rolldown}}
- \underbrace{(\tau-\Delta)\big[y_{t+\Delta}(\tau-\Delta) - y_t(\tau-\Delta)\big]}_{\text{duration}\times\text{yield change}} ,
$$ {#eq-22-return}

an identity obtained by adding and subtracting $(\tau-\Delta)\,y_t(\tau-\Delta)$.
The first term is the yield earned by standing still, the second what the bond
gains by sliding down an upward-sloping curve that does not move, and the third
the loss from a rise in the yield at the bond's new maturity, scaled by that
maturity. @ilmanen2011 treats the first two as the expected return of a bond on
an unchanged curve, and @koijen2018 show that the same carry logic prices assets
well beyond bonds. The scale factor on the yield change is the **duration** of
@macaulay1938, the maturity for a zero-coupon bond; the simple return $e^{r}-1$
adds the second-order **convexity** term $\tfrac{1}{2}(\tau-\Delta)^2(\Delta y)^2$,
positive whichever way yields move. In the modeled market every government bond
is a zero-coupon bond held at a constant maturity of two, five or ten years
(@sec-90-data-description-instruments), so its duration is known rather than
estimated, a gift for teaching and a limitation for realism.

The third term of @eq-22-return is why a bond portfolio is a set of exposures.
Suppose the yield changes at all maturities are driven by $K$ factors,
$\Delta y(\tau) = \sum_k b_k(\tau)\,\Delta f_k$. A portfolio with weights
$w_i$ in bonds of maturities $\tau_i$ then earns, up to carry and rolldown,

$$
r_p \approx -\sum_{k=1}^{K} \beta_k\, \Delta f_k,
\qquad
\beta_k = \sum_{i} w_i\, \tau_i\, b_k(\tau_i),
$$ {#eq-22-exposure}

and the weights matter only through the $K$ numbers $\beta_k$. Two portfolios
with the same exposures have the same risk, whatever bonds they hold. With
$K=3$ this is the finding of @litterman1991, and it is the reason the sleeve
below is specified as a set of exposures rather than as a set of weights.

### Three factors of the curve

@nelson1987 write the whole curve at a date as

$$
y_t(\tau) = L_t
+ S_t\,\frac{1-e^{-\lambda\tau}}{\lambda\tau}
+ C_t\left(\frac{1-e^{-\lambda\tau}}{\lambda\tau} - e^{-\lambda\tau}\right),
$$ {#eq-22-ns}

with loadings that @diebold2006 read as level, slope and curvature: the
loading on $L_t$ is one at every maturity, the loading on $S_t$ falls from one
at the short end to zero at the long end, so that $S_t$ is the short rate
minus the long rate, and the loading on $C_t$ is a hump that peaks in the
middle. @diebold2006 fix the decay $\lambda$ at $0.0609$ per month, which puts
the hump at thirty months, estimate the factors by least squares at each date,
and show that they track three observable quantities almost perfectly: the long
yield, the short minus the long yield, and twice a middle yield minus the two
ends. @litterman1991 reached the same three factors without a functional form,
as the first three principal components of yield changes, the first explaining
about ninety percent of the variance. With three maturities and three factors,
as here, any three-factor description is an exact rotation of the three yields;
which rotation the data ship, @sec-22-fixed-income-sleeve-implementation
measures. The rank deficiency of the bond block in
@sec-07-covariance-matrix-theory is the same fact seen from the covariance
matrix: five curves of three factors span the fifteen government bonds, and one
credit factor per region spans the credit bonds with them.

### Credit as a separate exposure

A corporate bond of maturity $\tau$ yields the government rate plus a spread
$s_t(\tau)$, so its price is $e^{-\tau(y_t + s_t)}$ and @eq-22-return acquires
a fourth term, $-(\tau-\Delta)\,\Delta s$: the **spread duration**, which for
a zero-coupon bond equals its duration. @merton1974 explains the spread as the
value of the default option the bondholder has written; @elton2001 show that
the expected loss from default explains only a small part of it, with taxes
and a premium for systematic risk making up the rest; and @collindufresne2001
find that spread changes across issuers are driven mostly by one common factor,
which is also how this market is built: the two grades of a region share one
credit factor. Two features matter for the sleeve. The spread is persistent: the weekly first-order autocorrelation of the US
investment-grade spread is
0.990,
a half-life of
67
weeks, so a spread that widens in a crisis stays wide for as long as the
credit cycle does. And the volatility of a spread is roughly proportional to
its level, which is why @bendor2007 measure credit exposure as duration times
spread rather than as duration alone: in this market the weekly changes of the
US high-yield spread have
3.4
times the standard deviation of the investment-grade changes.

### Duration targeting as a constrained optimization

The classical use of duration is immunization: @fisher1971 showed that a bond
portfolio whose duration equals the investor's horizon is protected, to first
order, against a parallel shift of the curve. A duration target is therefore a
linear constraint on the weights, $\sum_i w_i D_i = \bar D$, and minimizing
variance subject to it is still a quadratic program of the kind
@sec-12-constraints-theory and @sec-13-solvers-theory solve. In
`PortfolioAnalytics` such a constraint is a `factor_exposure` constraint with
the durations as the exposure vector $\boldsymbol{B}$: the package has no
notion of a bond, and does not need one, because by @eq-22-exposure a duration
target is a bound on the portfolio's loading on the level factor, and a second
column bounds the loading on the slope, which decides whether the duration is
delivered by a bullet at the middle of the curve or a barbell of its ends. The
level $\bar D$ is strategic: for a long-horizon investor @campbell2002 argue
that the long bond, not the bill, is the riskless asset, and how much duration
the policy portfolio carries is a decision of that kind. The deviation from
$\bar D$ conditioned on the curve is tactical, and
@sec-22-fixed-income-sleeve-implementation writes it as the parametric policy
of @sec-18-parametric-policies-theory.

### Currency, and why the two decisions are not separable abroad

Every series is in dollars, so a foreign bond carries its local return and its
currency's move together, and @sec-04-descriptive-analysis-application showed
that how much of a foreign holding is currency depends on the asset. For a
bond it is most of it:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
fx_share <- function(series, region) {
  f <- sim_fx_monthly[sim_fx_monthly$region == region, ]
  stopifnot(all(f$date == dates))
  u <- as.numeric(R[, series])
  1 - stats::var(u - f$fx_return) / stats::var(u)          # @eq-04-fx: share removed by hedging
}
round(c(JP_government = fx_share("JP_government", "JP"),
        EU_government = fx_share("EU_government", "EU")), 3)
#> JP_government EU_government 
#>         0.916         0.842
```
:::


Hedging removes 92%
of the variance of `JP_government`: a dollar investor who buys a Japanese bond
for its duration takes a currency position several times the size of the
interest-rate position. That is the case for fully hedging bonds that
@campbell2010 make and the "free lunch" of @perold1988; @black1989 argues for a
universal partial hedge, and @karnosky1994 attribute the result to the two
decisions separately. For the sleeve the consequence is that the duration and
currency decisions cannot be taken one at a time: an unhedged foreign bond is a
currency position with a small duration attached, and
@sec-22-fixed-income-sleeve-implementation measures what that does to the fit
of the curve factors.

### Predictability from the curve

The tactical case rests on the finding that the shape of the curve forecasts
bond returns. @fama1987 showed that forward spreads forecast the excess return
of long bonds over short ones; @campbell1991 showed that the yield spread
forecasts long-bond returns in the direction opposite to the expectations
hypothesis; @cochrane2005 found that a single combination of forward rates
forecasts the excess returns on bonds of every maturity with $R^2$ up to about
forty percent; and @fama1989 placed the term spread among the business-cycle
predictors of both stock and bond returns.
@sec-16-signals-and-forecasts-application tested the term spread on this
market and found it the one signal whose out-of-sample $R^2$ survives, which
is the signal the duration overlay below conditions on.

## Measuring and Targeting the Exposures {#sec-22-fixed-income-sleeve-implementation}

### The factor series and their units

Nothing in a column of numbers says whether a level of four is four percent or
four hundred, so the units are read from the magnitudes before anything is
computed from them.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
units <- sim_curve_weekly |>
  dplyr::mutate(kind = sub("^[A-Z]+_", "", series)) |>
  dplyr::group_by(kind) |>
  dplyr::summarise(median_abs = median(abs(value)), max_abs = max(abs(value)))
units
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   kind      median_abs max_abs
#>   <chr>          <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 Curvature    0.193    1.58  
#> 2 HY_Spread    0.0191   0.156 
#> 3 IG_Spread    0.00468  0.0580
#> 4 Level        2.74    10     
#> 5 Slope        0.873    3.05
lsc <- grep("_(Level|Slope|Curvature)$", names(cv), value = TRUE)
stopifnot(units$max_abs[units$kind == "Level"] > 1,              # a level of 8 is 8 percent
          all(units$max_abs[grepl("Spread", units$kind)] < 1))   # a spread of 0.14 is 14 percent
cv[lsc] <- cv[lsc] / 100                                          # decimals from here on
```
:::


The level reaches 10.0,
which can only be percentage points, and the spreads peak at
0.16, which can
only be a decimal, as @sec-16-signals-and-forecasts-implementation also found;
the chunk puts everything in decimals so that a loading is a duration in years.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Level, slope and curvature of the US curve, weekly, in percentage points. The slope is the short end minus the long end, so an inverted curve shows as a positive slope. The shaded bands are the four episodes of `sim_episodes`.](22-fixed-income-sleeve_files/figure-html/fig-22-factors-1.png){#fig-22-factors fig-align='center' width=90%}
:::
:::


### Factor exposures, and which bond is which

The exposures of @eq-22-exposure are regression coefficients: each
instrument's weekly return on the weekly changes of its region's level, slope
and curvature, and for credit also of its grade's spread. Each regression is
run twice, on the return as shipped and on the hedged return, which subtracts
the region's `fx_return`.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
dcv <- as.data.frame(lapply(cv[-1], diff))                 # factor changes, aligned with the returns
exposure <- function(id) {
  rg <- bonds$region[bonds$asset_id == id]; gr <- bonds$credit_grade[bonds$asset_id == id]
  X  <- data.frame(level = dcv[[paste0(rg, "_Level")]], slope = dcv[[paste0(rg, "_Slope")]],
                   curvature = dcv[[paste0(rg, "_Curvature")]],
                   spread = if (is.na(gr)) 0 else dcv[[paste0(rg, "_", gr, "_Spread")]])
  f   <- if (rg == "US") 0 else fx[[rg]]
  fml <- if (is.na(gr)) y ~ level + slope + curvature else y ~ level + slope + curvature + spread
  mh  <- stats::lm(fml, data = cbind(y = as.numeric(A[, id]) - f, X))   # hedged
  mu  <- stats::lm(fml, data = cbind(y = as.numeric(A[, id]),     X))   # unhedged, as shipped
  b   <- stats::coef(mh)
  tibble::tibble(asset = id, region = rg, class = bonds$asset_class[bonds$asset_id == id],
                 grade = ifelse(is.na(gr), "", gr),
                 level = b[["level"]], slope = b[["slope"]], curvature = b[["curvature"]],
                 spread = if (is.na(gr)) NA_real_ else b[["spread"]],
                 r2_hedged = summary(mh)$r.squared, r2_unhedged = summary(mu)$r.squared)
}
expo <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(colnames(A), exposure))
```
:::


`sim_assets` carries no maturity, so which instrument is the two-, five- or
ten-year has to be inferred, and @eq-22-return says how: the loading on the
level is minus the duration, and the ten-year is the most rate-sensitive bond
of its region and grade. The inference is asserted rather than assumed, by
requiring every implied duration to lie within ten percent of the maturity it
has been assigned.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
expo <- expo |>
  dplyr::group_by(region, class, grade) |>
  dplyr::mutate(maturity = c(10, 5, 2)[rank(level)]) |>      # most negative loading: the ten-year
  dplyr::ungroup()
stopifnot(all(abs(-expo$level / expo$maturity - 1) < 0.10),
          all(table(expo$region, expo$maturity) == 3L))      # three bonds per maturity and region
mat <- setNames(expo$maturity, expo$asset)
id_of <- function(rg, tau, cls = "government", gr = "")
  expo$asset[expo$region == rg & expo$class == cls & expo$grade == gr & expo$maturity == tau]
```
:::

The level loadings of the government bonds in @tbl-22-exposures are
-1.92, -4.80, -9.58,
minus the maturity divided by one plus the yield: the modified duration under
annual compounding, so the bonds are repriced in full rather than through the
first-order term of @eq-22-return. The credit bonds have the same durations and
a spread duration of the same size, as the theory says, and every $R^2$ is
0.970 or better: a US
bond is spanned by the factors up to the time variation of its carry, the rank
deficiency of @sec-07-covariance-matrix-theory seen one instrument at a time.

The slope and curvature columns reveal which rotation of the three yields the
factors are: the ten-year loads on the level alone, the two-year equally on
level and slope, the five-year on the level and half of the slope and half of
the curvature.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
B_hat <- expo |>
  dplyr::filter(class == "government") |>
  dplyr::group_by(maturity) |>
  dplyr::summarise(slope = mean(slope / level), curvature = mean(curvature / level)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(level = 1, .after = maturity)                # loadings relative to the level loading
B_hat
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   maturity level    slope curvature
#>      <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1        2     1  1.00     0.000242
#> 2        5     1  0.498    0.498   
#> 3       10     1 -0.00348  0.00137
B_emp <- rbind(`2` = c(1, 1, 0), `5` = c(1, 0.5, 0.5), `10` = c(1, 0, 0))
stopifnot(max(abs(as.matrix(B_hat[, -1]) - B_emp)) < 0.05)
```
:::


So the shipped factors are the observable level, slope and curvature that
@diebold2006 use to interpret their latent ones: the ten-year yield, the
two-year minus the ten-year, and twice the five-year minus the two- and
ten-year. The latent loadings of @eq-22-ns at the Diebold–Li decay, three lines
of code, are a different rotation of the same three yields, and the exposures of
@eq-22-exposure transform with the rotation while the risk they describe does
not.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
lam <- 0.0609 * 12                                            # Diebold-Li decay, per year
ns_load <- function(tau) cbind(level = 1, slope = (1 - exp(-lam * tau)) / (lam * tau),
                               curvature = (1 - exp(-lam * tau)) / (lam * tau) - exp(-lam * tau))
yields <- function(rg) {                                       # the three yields, from B_emp
  F <- as.matrix(cv[, paste0(rg, c("_Level", "_Slope", "_Curvature"))])
  Y <- F %*% t(B_emp); colnames(Y) <- c("y2", "y5", "y10"); Y
}
Y_us <- yields("US")
round(ns_load(c(2, 5, 10)), 3)                                 # latent loadings at 2, 5 and 10 years
#>      level slope curvature
#> [1,]     1 0.526     0.294
#> [2,]     1 0.267     0.241
#> [3,]     1 0.137     0.136
```
:::


The principal components of @litterman1991 are the third description, and the
one that needs no functional form at all.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
pc <- stats::prcomp(diff(Y_us))
share <- summary(pc)$importance["Proportion of Variance", ]
round(share, 3)
#>   PC1   PC2   PC3 
#> 0.913 0.073 0.014
round(pc$rotation, 2)
#>      PC1   PC2   PC3
#> y2  0.52 -0.77  0.38
#> y5  0.63  0.04 -0.78
#> y10 0.58  0.64  0.50
stopifnot(length(unique(sign(pc$rotation[, 1]))) == 1L,            # a level: all one sign
          sign(pc$rotation["y2", 2]) != sign(pc$rotation["y10", 2]), # a slope: ends opposed
          sign(pc$rotation["y5", 3]) != sign(pc$rotation["y2", 3]))  # a curvature: middle opposed
```
:::


The first component moves all three yields the same way and carries
91.3% of the variance of weekly yield
changes; the second opposes the two ends and carries
7.3%; the third opposes the middle to the
ends and carries the remaining 1.4%, within
a few points of the proportions @litterman1991 report.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Worked: the week the ten-year moved most

@eq-22-return is checked on the week in which the US ten-year yield moved most,
with $y^{c} = \log(1+y)$ the continuously compounded yield.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
yc  <- log(1 + Y_us[, "y10"])                                  # continuously compounded
i   <- which.max(abs(diff(yc)))                                # the week of the largest move
dy  <- diff(yc)[i]; y0 <- yc[i]; tau <- 10; d <- 1 / 52
r_actual <- as.numeric(A[i, id_of("US", 10)])
carry    <- d * y0
duration <- -(tau - d) * dy
convexity <- 0.5 * (tau - d)^2 * dy^2
round(c(yield_change_bp = 1e4 * dy, carry = carry, duration = duration,
        convexity = convexity, first_order = carry + duration,
        second_order = carry + duration + convexity, actual = r_actual), 5)
#> yield_change_bp           carry        duration       convexity     first_order 
#>        53.15923         0.00060        -0.05306         0.00141        -0.05245 
#>    second_order          actual 
#>        -0.05105        -0.05084
```
:::


In May of model year 18 the ten-year yield rose by
53 basis points. Substituting into @eq-22-return,

$$
r \approx \underbrace{\tfrac{1}{52}\times 0.0314}_{\text{carry}}
\;-\; \underbrace{9.981 \times 0.00532}_{\text{duration}}
\;+\; \underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2}\times 99.62 \times 0.00532^{\,2}}_{\text{convexity}}
= -0.0510,
$$

against an actual return of -0.0508. The duration term
is the whole of the move, the convexity gives back
14 basis points of the loss, and the
2
basis points that remain are that week's rolldown and the error of the
expansion.
:::

### What the currency does to the fit

Outside the US the same regressions tell two stories.

|region | D (2y)| D (5y)| D (10y)| R² hedged| R² unhedged|
|:------|------:|------:|-------:|---------:|-----------:|
|US     |   1.92|   4.80|    9.58|     0.988|       0.988|
|UK     |   1.89|   4.75|    9.51|     0.988|       0.173|
|CH     |   1.97|   4.90|    9.75|     0.988|       0.151|

Hedged, the foreign government bonds are explained by their own curves as well
as the US bonds are, a mean $R^2$ of 0.959 across
the four regions, the lowest JP_GOV_01 at
0.696. Unhedged, the mean is
0.144: the same local return sits inside a
currency move that explains most of the variance, the share computed in
@sec-22-fixed-income-sleeve-theory, so a duration target set on an unhedged
foreign sleeve controls a minority of its risk.

### The sleeve as a set of exposures

The sleeve is the fifteen government bonds, weekly and unhedged, and the
duration is a `factor_exposure` constraint whose $\boldsymbol{B}$ holds the
duration of each bond from the level loadings above. The matrix is bound to the
asset names and the binding asserted, for the reason the callout below gives;
every bound is widened by a millionth of a year, for the reason the callout in
@sec-22-fixed-income-sleeve-application gives.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
gov <- expo$asset[expo$class == "government"]
G   <- A[, gov]
B   <- cbind(duration = -expo$level, slope = -expo$slope)[match(gov, expo$asset), ]
rownames(B) <- gov
stopifnot(identical(rownames(B), colnames(G)))
sleeve <- function(assets, B, lower, upper = lower, band = 1e-6) {
  stopifnot(identical(if (is.matrix(B)) rownames(B) else names(B), assets))
  portfolio.spec(assets) |>
    add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
    add.constraint(type = "long_only") |>
    add.constraint(type = "factor_exposure", B = B,            # band: the application says why
                   lower = lower - band, upper = upper + band) |>
    add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var")
}
exposures <- function(w) setNames(as.numeric(t(w[rownames(B)]) %*% B), colnames(B))
ann_vol   <- function(w) sqrt(as.numeric(t(w) %*% stats::cov(G) %*% w) * 52)

w_free <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(G, sleeve(gov, B[, "duration"], 0, 20),
                                            optimize_method = "ROI"))
w_five <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(G, sleeve(gov, B[, "duration"], 5),
                                            optimize_method = "ROI"))
round(w_free[w_free > 0.005], 3)
#> UK_GOV_01 US_GOV_01 
#>     0.005     0.995
round(w_five[w_five > 0.005], 3)
#> CH_GOV_03 EU_GOV_03 JP_GOV_03 UK_GOV_03 US_GOV_01 US_GOV_03 
#>     0.008     0.018     0.106     0.057     0.600     0.212
rbind(unconstrained = c(exposures(w_free), vol = ann_vol(w_free)),
      duration_5    = c(exposures(w_five), vol = ann_vol(w_five))) |> round(3)
#>               duration slope   vol
#> unconstrained    1.922 1.919 0.016
#> duration_5       5.000 1.133 0.038
```
:::


Left to itself, minimum variance holds the US two-year and almost nothing else, at a
duration of 1.92: the least volatile bond
is the shortest one in the home currency, and the argument of
@sec-09-mean-variance-application applies unchanged. Told to carry a duration
of five, the optimizer delivers it as a **barbell**: the US two-year and
ten-year carry 81%
of the portfolio between them, with
19% in
foreign ten-year bonds whose currency moves diversify the dollar curve, and
the five-year is not held at all. The duration is met exactly, and the slope
exposure that comes with it is 1.13.

::: {.callout-warning}
## `factor_exposure_constraint()` binds `B` by position, not by name

The constructor checks that `B` has as many rows as there are assets and
nothing else: row names are stored, never compared with the asset names. A
`B` whose rows are in a different order than `colnames(R)` is accepted and the
constraint is applied to the wrong bonds.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
B_rev  <- B[rev(rownames(B)), "duration"]                    # same numbers, reversed order
w_rev  <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(G, sleeve(rev(gov), B_rev, 5),
                                            optimize_method = "ROI"))
c(what_the_solver_believed = 5, true_duration = sum(w_rev * B[names(w_rev), "duration"]))
#> what_the_solver_believed            true_duration 
#>                    5.000                    4.903
```
:::


The solver reports a duration of five and the portfolio has one of
4.90. `sleeve()`
refuses a `B` whose names are not identical to the assets in the order of the
return matrix, the rule of @sec-09-mean-variance-implementation applied to a
constraint; `random_portfolios()` ignores factor-exposure bounds altogether,
which @sec-28-robustness-implementation returns to.
:::

A second column of $\boldsymbol{B}$ bounds the slope exposure. With the
duration fixed, the slope decides *where* on the curve the duration sits.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
w_bullet <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(G, sleeve(gov, B, lower = c(5, 2), upper = c(5, 2.5)),
                                              optimize_method = "ROI"))
round(w_bullet[w_bullet > 0.005], 3)
#> CH_GOV_03 JP_GOV_03 UK_GOV_02 UK_GOV_03 US_GOV_01 US_GOV_02 
#>     0.007     0.085     0.016     0.036     0.147     0.709
rbind(barbell = c(exposures(w_five), vol = ann_vol(w_five)),
      bullet  = c(exposures(w_bullet), vol = ann_vol(w_bullet))) |> round(3)
#>         duration slope   vol
#> barbell        5 1.133 0.038
#> bullet         5 2.000 0.042
```
:::


Requiring a slope exposure of at least two pushes the sleeve into the
five-year, a **bullet**, at the same duration and a volatility of
4.15% against
3.83% for the barbell: the same
exposure to a parallel shift, different exposures to a twist, and on this
sample the ends of the curve hedged each other better than the middle hedged
itself.

A bound the bonds cannot meet is the last case. No long-only combination of
two-, five- and ten-year bonds has a duration of twelve:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
o_bad <- optimize.portfolio(G, sleeve(gov, B[, "duration"], 12), optimize_method = "ROI")
c(class = class(o_bad)[1], weights_are_na = anyNA(o_bad$weights), status = o_bad$solver_status)
#>                                        class 
#>                     "optimize.portfolio.ROI" 
#>                               weights_are_na 
#>                                       "TRUE" 
#>                                       status 
#> "Constraints are inconsistent, no solution."
```
:::


No error and no warning: the object has the usual class, weights of `NA` and
the solver's message stored inside it. In a rebalancing loop this is a period
of `NA`, the failure @sec-25-backtesting-implementation is built to catch, and
the application uses `pm_backtest()` for that reason.

### The duration overlay as a parametric policy

The tactical layer is written as the policy of @eq-18-policy with one
characteristic. Let $z_t$ be the US term spread, the ten-year less the
two-year yield, standardized, and let the long end of the sleeve be the US
ten-year and the short end the US two-year. The weight on the long end is

$$
w_t = \bar w + \theta\, z_t,
\qquad
\hat\theta = \arg\max_\theta \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t} u\!\big(w_t\, r^{10}_{t+1} + (1-w_t)\, r^{2}_{t+1}\big),
$$ {#eq-22-overlay}

with $u$ the power utility of @eq-18-estimator at $\gamma = 5$. The anchor
$\bar w$ is the strategic decision, set so that the policy at $z_t = 0$ has the
duration of the equal-weighted two-, five- and ten-year ladder, which is the
class series the allocation sees; $\theta$ is the tactical one. The data are
monthly, with the curve read at each month end from the last weekly observation
of that month, as @sec-16-signals-and-forecasts-implementation does.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
i_last <- findInterval(dates, cv$date)                      # last weekly curve point in each month
stopifnot(all(format(cv$date[i_last], "%Y-%m") == format(dates, "%Y-%m")))
term    <- -cv$US_Slope[i_last]                             # ten-year less two-year, decimal
r_long  <- as.numeric(Am[, id_of("US", 10)])
r_short <- as.numeric(Am[, id_of("US", 2)])
gamma   <- 5
D_bar   <- mean(c(2, 5, 10))                                # the ladder's duration, in years
w_bar   <- (D_bar - 2) / (10 - 2)                           # long-end weight that delivers it
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
crra <- function(r) (1 + r)^(1 - gamma) / (1 - gamma)
policy_utility <- function(theta, z, rl, rs) {
  w <- w_bar + theta * z
  mean(crra(w * rl + (1 - w) * rs))                         # @eq-22-overlay
}
z <- (term - mean(term)) / stats::sd(term)
# the signal at t sits beside the return of t + 1: z[-Tn] against r[-1]
fit_theta <- function(i) stats::optimize(policy_utility, c(-3, 3), z = z[-Tn][i],
                                         rl = r_long[-1][i], rs = r_short[-1][i],
                                         maximum = TRUE)$maximum
theta_hat <- fit_theta(seq_len(Tn - 1L))

set.seed(1602)
block_index <- function(n, block = 12L) {                   # the block bootstrap of chapter 9
  starts <- sample.int(n - block + 1L, ceiling(n / block), replace = TRUE)
  as.vector(outer(0:(block - 1L), starts, "+"))[seq_len(n)]
}
boot  <- vapply(seq_len(500L), function(b) fit_theta(block_index(Tn - 1L)), numeric(1))
ce    <- function(theta)                                    # monthly certainty equivalent
  ((1 - gamma) * policy_utility(theta, z[-Tn], r_long[-1], r_short[-1]))^(1 / (1 - gamma)) - 1
round(c(theta = theta_hat, se_block_bootstrap = stats::sd(boot), t = theta_hat / stats::sd(boot),
        ce_gain_annual = 12 * (ce(theta_hat) - ce(0))), 3)
#>              theta se_block_bootstrap                  t     ce_gain_annual 
#>              0.715              0.461              1.553              0.007
```
:::


The fitted $\hat\theta$ is 0.72: one standard
deviation of term spread moves the long-end weight by
72 percentage points, or the duration by
5.7 years, in the direction @cochrane2005
predicts. Its block-bootstrap standard error [@kuensch1989] is
0.46, a $t$-statistic of
1.55, and the in-sample
certainty-equivalent gain over the constant policy is
0.74 percentage points a
year: the sign the literature predicts without the precision to be sure of it,
the usual state of a tactical signal [@welch2008].

## The Sleeve Out of Sample {#sec-22-fixed-income-sleeve-application}

The application runs from observation 121, the first out-of-sample month of
the register of @sec-25-backtesting-application, with a sixty-month window and
monthly rebalancing. One plain limitation first: the five government class
series are each the equal-weighted ladder of the same three maturities, so they
share one duration and a duration target cannot be set on them. The sleeves
therefore run on the fifteen government instruments behind those classes and
are judged against the class series. The **equal-weighted sleeve** holds the
five government class series equally, the benchmark the allocation sees, with a
duration of 5.67. The **constant-duration sleeve** is
minimum variance on the fifteen instruments with the duration bound to that
same 5.67, the durations being the maturities, which need
no estimation. The **duration overlay** is the same optimization with the
target moved by the policy of @eq-22-overlay, re-estimated every month on the
data available then. And **credit** enters as a separate exposure: the five
credit class series join the universe with a second column of
$\boldsymbol{B}$, the spread duration, bound so that the sleeve carries the
duration and the spread duration of an equal-weighted portfolio of all ten bond
classes, its benchmark.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
tilt <- vapply(120:Tn, function(t) {                           # everything indexed <= t
  zt <- (term[1:t] - mean(term[1:t])) / stats::sd(term[1:t])
  th <- stats::optimize(policy_utility, c(-3, 3), z = zt[-t],
                        rl = r_long[2:t], rs = r_short[2:t], maximum = TRUE)$maximum
  th * zt[t]
}, numeric(1))
w_long <- pmin(pmax(w_bar + tilt, 0), 1)                     # long only: clipped at the ends
D_path <- setNames(2 + 8 * w_long, as.character(dates[120:Tn]))   # one target per rebalancing date
round(c(min = min(D_path), mean = mean(D_path), max = max(D_path),
        share_at_a_bound = mean(w_long %in% c(0, 1))), 2)
#>              min             mean              max share_at_a_bound 
#>             2.00             5.59            10.00             0.21
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![The duration target of the overlay at each rebalancing date, set from the term spread with the policy re-estimated on the data available at that date. The dashed line is the constant target; the shaded bands are the episodes.](22-fixed-income-sleeve_files/figure-html/fig-22-duration-1.png){#fig-22-duration fig-align='center' width=90%}
:::
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
oos  <- 61:Tn                      # a 60-month window ending at 120 puts the first OOS month at 121
cost_of <- setNames(unname(pm_costs_default()[sim_assets$asset_class]), sim_assets$asset_id)
gov_cl <- grep("_government$", colnames(R), value = TRUE)
cre_cl <- grep("_credit$",     colnames(R), value = TRUE)
ew_spec <- function(assets) portfolio.spec(assets) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |> add.constraint(type = "long_only")

equal_weight <- pm_strategy("equal_weight", spec = ew_spec, weight_fun = equal.weight,
                            metric = "sharpe", label = "Equal weight")
constant_duration <- pm_strategy("constant_duration", optimize_method = "ROI",
  spec  = function(assets) sleeve(assets, mat[assets], D_bar),
  label = "Constant duration")
overlay <- pm_strategy("overlay", label = "Duration overlay",
  spec  = function(assets) sleeve(assets, mat[assets], D_bar),
  weight_fun = function(R, portfolio, ...) {                 # R is the window ending at the rebalance
    D <- D_path[[as.character(zoo::index(R)[nrow(R)])]]
    optimize.portfolio(R, sleeve(colnames(R), mat[colnames(R)], D), optimize_method = "ROI")
  })
U_cre <- cbind(Am[oos, gov], R[oos, cre_cl])
B_cre <- cbind(duration = c(mat[gov], setNames(rep(D_bar, 5), cre_cl)),
               spread   = c(setNames(rep(0, 15), gov), setNames(rep(D_bar, 5), cre_cl)))
with_credit <- pm_strategy("with_credit", optimize_method = "ROI",
  spec  = function(assets) sleeve(assets, B_cre[assets, ], c(D_bar, D_bar / 2)),
  label = "Constant duration plus credit")

run <- function(X, ..., costs = pm_costs_default())
  pm_backtest(X, pm_register(...), riskfree = sim_riskfree_monthly, estimation_window = 60L,
              costs = costs, verbose = FALSE)
bt <- list(
  ew_gov = run(R[oos, gov_cl], equal_weight),
  sleeve = run(Am[oos, gov], constant_duration, overlay, costs = cost_of[gov]),
  ew_all = run(R[oos, c(gov_cl, cre_cl)], equal_weight),
  credit = run(U_cre, with_credit, costs = c(cost_of[gov], credit = pm_costs_default()[["credit"]]))
)
labels <- c(ew_gov = "Equal weight, five government classes", ew_all = "Equal weight, ten bond classes")
mets <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(bt), function(k) {
  m <- bt[[k]]$metrics
  if (k %in% names(labels)) m$label <- labels[[k]]
  dplyr::mutate(m, key = k, .before = 1)                     # two strategies share a name
}))
stopifnot(all(mets$n_failed == 0L), all(vapply(bt, function(b) b$meta$oos_start, Sys.Date()) == dates[121]))
```
:::

G_oos  <- Am[oos, gov]
ends   <- 60:nrow(G_oos)                                     # the rebalancing dates of the backtest
failed <- vapply(ends, function(e) {                         # the same windows, lower == upper
  w <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(G_oos[(e - 59):e, ],
                                         sleeve(gov, mat[gov], D_bar, band = 0),
                                         optimize_method = "ROI"))
  anyNA(w)
}, logical(1))
stopifnot(length(ends) == bt$sleeve$metrics$n_periods[1])
c(windows = length(ends), failed_with_exact_target = sum(failed))
#>                  windows failed_with_exact_target

::: {.callout-important}
## An exact exposure target can be reported infeasible in a third of the windows

The `band` argument of `sleeve()` is not cosmetic. With `band = 0`, the exposure
equality reaches `quadprog` as two opposing inequalities, the same degeneracy
that @sec-09-mean-variance-implementation documents for `full_investment`, and
on these fifteen bonds 89 of the 253 rolling windows
come back with the message
seen above and weights of `NA`; the same windows solve once the bounds are a
millionth of a year apart. `pm_backtest()` counts such periods in `n_failed`
and carries the previous weights forward, and the assertion above requires the
count to be zero, so that the table below describes the strategy that was
specified.
:::

In the credit crisis the ten-year yield fell by

The class series the allocation of @sec-15-hierarchical-allocation-theory
sees, `US_government` and its four siblings, is the equal-weighted ladder, and
that is the sleeve's benchmark: the allocation decides how much of the
portfolio is government bonds, and the sleeve's job is a set of exposures
relative to the ladder, a duration, a position on the curve, a spread
duration, each written here as a bound on a factor loading. The package can
nest the sleeve under the allocation itself, through `mult.portfolio.spec()`
and `add.sub.portfolio()`, which optimize each sleeve on its own rebalancing
calendar and allocate across the proxy return series; exercise 4 runs it and
finds the proxies back-filled with equal weights before the first rebalance,
the trap of @sec-23-rebalancing-implementation. The same loadings are what a
scenario needs: @sec-965-scenario-analysis shocks the level, the slope and the
spreads directly and reads off, through @eq-22-exposure, what every sleeve and
every class does. What the exposures cost to maintain is the subject of
@sec-23-rebalancing-theory, and whether the overlay's single sample is evidence
is the subject of @sec-25-backtesting-theory.

## Key Takeaways {.unnumbered}

- A bond's return is carry plus rolldown minus duration times the yield change,
  @eq-22-return, so a bond portfolio is a set of exposures to the factors that
  move yields, and two portfolios with the same exposures have the same
  interest-rate risk whatever bonds they hold [@litterman1991].
- Three factors describe the curve. The modeled market ships the observable
  level, slope and curvature of @diebold2006, a rotation of the two-, five- and
  ten-year yields; the principal components of yield changes recover the same
  three shapes.
- A duration target is a `factor_exposure` constraint on the level loading, a
  second column decides between barbell and bullet, and minimum variance subject
  to both is still a quadratic program. `B` is bound by position, an exact
  target can be reported infeasible, and an infeasible one returns `NA` weights
  without a warning.
- For a dollar investor a foreign government bond is mostly currency: hedged,
  the curve factors explain it as well as a US bond; unhedged, a fraction of it.
  The duration and currency decisions are taken together or not at all
  [@campbell2010].
- The duration overlay is the parametric policy of chapter 18 with one
  characteristic: the sign the literature predicts, a $t$-statistic below two,
  and out of sample the smallest loss in the rates shock because the curve had
  flattened first, which is one episode.
